title: Sparing Saul (1 Samuel 24)
hookLine: David cuts Saul's robe in the cave but will not harm him
carry: I will not put forth my hand

lines: THIS IS THE DAY, THEY SAY.
cards: A cave in the wilderness of En-gedi, wild-goat country. Deep inside, in the dark, David and his men are hiding from the king who wants him dead.

Then the king himself walks in, alone, to relieve himself, with no idea who's at the back of the cave. David's men lean in and whisper: this is the day God promised. Your enemy, delivered into your hand.
Do to him whatever seems good to you. David gets up, and creeps forward in the dark.

teach.b: He reaches Saul and quietly cuts off the corner of his robe. That's all.
And then, the text says, David's heart struck him, because he had cut off Saul's skirt. Robes matter in this book.

Earlier, when Saul grabbed the prophet Samuel's robe and it tore, Samuel told him the kingdom had been torn from him the same way. So a torn corner of the king's robe is no small thing. David turns to his men: God forbid.
I will not put forth my hand against my lord, because he is the Lord's anointed. He holds them back, and Saul walks out unharmed. Then David takes a risk.
He follows, calls after Saul, bows to the ground, and holds up the corner of the robe. I was close enough to cut this, and I didn't kill you.

teach.h: I WILL NOT PUT FORTH MY HAND.
teach.b: Let the Lord judge between us, but my hand won't be on you. And Saul, the hunter, weeps aloud.

teach.h: IS THIS YOUR VOICE, MY SON?
teach.b: Is this your voice, my son David? He says David is more righteous than he is, because David repaid him good for evil. Here's what makes this hard.
David's men use religious language: this is the day God promised. David answers with religious language too: the Lord's anointed. Same God, opposite conclusions.
The text sides with the one who keeps his hand still, and it notices that even the small cut hurt his conscience.

how: Jews read David sparing Saul in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and some teachers read it alongside the Torah's warnings against taking revenge or bearing a grudge.

o: David's men hiding the king from the Philistines
David letting the king who hunts him go unharmed
Saul ending his hunt for David once and for all

p: the wilderness where the cave is
Saul's words when David calls out

s: David felt no regret, since he only cut cloth
the text says his heart struck him because he had cut off Saul's skirt.
Saul wept when David called out to him
he lifted up his voice and wept, and said David was more righteous than he was.
David's men urged him to let Saul go
they told him this was the day God had promised to deliver his enemy into his hand.

games.q: you're David. the king who's hunting you is alone in the cave, a few steps away. your men say this is the day. what do you do?
o: cut a corner of his robe and let him go.
slip out the back and keep running.
games.why: he cuts the corner of the robe, then regrets even that, holds his men back, and calls after Saul to show him he spared him.

practice: Let someone come to mind who has wronged you, or who's simply in your power right now: a person whose secret you know, whose weak spot you could press.

Notice the voices that say this is the day, then picture your hand staying still; you don't have to forgive them now, just choose not to cut. If you pray, you can hold David's words: I will not put forth my hand.

wordCard.voice: Sparing Saul. A king in the dark, a corner of his robe, and a hand that stays still. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: I will not send out my hand, David's words in the cave.

carryVoice: Your line: I will not put forth my hand. Even when the chance is right there. That's day seven hundred forty.
